title: What is the DRY ("Don't Repeat Yourself") principle, how do you follow it, and how should it be applied carefully in microservices?
shortTitle: The DRY ("Don't Repeat Yourself") principle, how to follow it, and applying it carefully in microservices

s1_definition.profdef: DRY stands for Don't Repeat Yourself. It states that every piece of knowledge or logic in a system should have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation. The goal is that when a rule changes, you change it in exactly one place. DRY applies not just to duplicated code but to duplicated business knowledge, constants, validation rules, and data definitions. Crucially, DRY is about avoiding duplication of knowledge, not merely duplication of characters that happen to look alike.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India's rule that a minimum balance in a savings account is five thousand rupees. If that number five thousand is written in the account-opening screen, again in the withdrawal check, again in the monthly fee calculation, and again in a report, then when the bank changes the minimum to ten thousand, someone has to find and fix all four places — and will surely miss one, causing bugs. DRY says: write that rule once, in one place, and have everyone ask that one place. Then changing it is a single, safe edit. Rajesh's minimum-balance rule lives in exactly one spot.
s1_definition.oneliner: Every rule or piece of knowledge should live in exactly one place, so a change is a single safe edit — but only unify things that are truly the same knowledge.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** DRY stands for Don't Repeat Yourself. It states that every piece of knowledge or logic in a system should have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation. The goal is that when a rule changes, you change it in exactly one place. DRY applies not just to duplicated code but to duplicated business knowledge, constants, validation rules, and data definitions. Crucially, DRY is about avoiding duplication of knowledge, not merely duplication of characters that happen to look alike.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India's rule that a minimum balance in a savings account is five thousand rupees. If that number five thousand is written in the account-opening screen, again in the withdrawal check, again in the monthly fee calculation, and again in a report, then when the bank changes the minimum to ten thousand, someone has to find and fix all four places — and will surely miss one, causing bugs. DRY says: write that rule once, in one place, and have everyone ask that one place. Then changing it is a single, safe edit. Rajesh's minimum-balance rule lives in exactly one spot.

**One line to remember:** Every rule or piece of knowledge should live in exactly one place, so a change is a single safe edit — but only unify things that are truly the same knowledge.

sections.s2_technical:
Following DRY starts with recognising duplication of knowledge. The most obvious form is copy-pasted code. If the same validation block appears in three methods, extract it into one method and call it from all three. If the same constant appears in many files, define it once, for example `public static final BigDecimal MIN_SAVINGS_BALANCE = new BigDecimal("5000");`, and reference that single constant everywhere so the rule has one home.

You follow DRY with several techniques. **Extract method** pulls repeated statements into a named method. **Extract class** pulls a repeated cluster of fields and behaviour into its own type. **Inheritance or composition** lets related classes share behaviour — though composition is usually safer than deep inheritance. **Generics** remove duplication across types, so one generic repository serves many entity types instead of one hand-written repository per entity. **Configuration** centralises values that would otherwise be scattered as literals. In Spring you also lean on shared components, base classes, and utility beans so cross-cutting logic lives once.

A key senior insight is distinguishing **true duplication from coincidental duplication**. Two code blocks that look identical today but represent different business rules are not real duplication. If you merge them just because they look alike, you create a false abstraction that becomes painful the moment the two rules diverge — now one change has to serve two masters, and you end up adding flags and conditionals to the shared code. This is why experienced engineers say "duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction." You wait until you see the same knowledge repeated enough times, and that the repetitions genuinely change together, before you unify them.

Now the microservices angle, which is where DRY gets genuinely tricky. Within a single service, DRY is a clear win. But across microservices, aggressively removing duplication can quietly destroy the very independence that microservices exist to provide. If you factor every shared piece into one library that all services import, then changing that library forces every service to upgrade and redeploy in lockstep, and an innocent change can break many services at once. You have recreated a distributed monolith. Similarly, sharing a single database schema or shared domain entities across services couples their data models so tightly that one team's change breaks another's. So in microservices, some duplication is deliberately accepted as the price of independence. Each service may keep its own copy of a DTO or a small validation rule so it can evolve independently.

The practical guidance is this. Share genuinely stable, generic, non-domain things across services — logging setup, security helpers, serialization utilities — ideally as versioned libraries so a service can upgrade on its own schedule rather than being forced. But do not share business logic or domain models across service boundaries; let each service own its model, even if that means a little duplication. Prefer communication over sharing: if two services need the same rule applied, often the service that owns that rule exposes it via an API rather than every service importing a shared implementation. And when you do create a shared library, version it carefully with backward compatibility so consumers are not forced into synchronised deployments. In short, DRY within a service, but tolerate and even prefer some duplication across services to protect their autonomy.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India had the minimum-balance rule and the overdraft-fee calculation copy-pasted into three different places: the withdrawal flow, the monthly-maintenance flow, and the statement generator. When the regulator changed the minimum balance, a developer updated two of the three and missed the statement generator, which then reported wrong fees to customers. This is exactly the pain DRY removes — the rule must live in one authoritative place so a change is a single edit.

Problem 2 — Within our single account service we want the rule centralised, but we also run a separate notification microservice. We must be careful: we should not force the notification service to import the account service's internal rule class, because that would couple the two services and force them to deploy together. So within the account service we apply DRY fully, and across the service boundary we keep things loosely coupled.

In the mini-project we will show the before-and-after of DRY inside one service. We will create a single `AccountPolicy` class that holds the minimum balance and the overdraft fee calculation in one place. The withdrawal logic and the fee logic both ask `AccountPolicy` rather than hard-coding numbers. We will run a withdrawal for Rajesh that respects the minimum balance and compute a maintenance fee for Priya, both driven by the single policy. Then we will change the minimum balance in one place and show both flows pick it up automatically.

The code contains: an `Account` model; a single `AccountPolicy` holding the rules; a `WithdrawalService` and a `MaintenanceService` that both consult the policy; and a `main` that runs both flows and then demonstrates a one-line rule change.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh with ten lakh, Priya with four thousand (below the five thousand minimum), and a single `AccountPolicy` holding the minimum balance and fee rate.

Step 1: One `AccountPolicy` is created with the minimum balance five thousand and fee rate two percent. Both the withdrawal service and the maintenance service receive this same policy. There is no number repeated across the services.

Step 2: Rajesh withdraws nine lakh ninety thousand. The withdrawal service asks the policy `allowsWithdrawal`, which checks that the resulting balance of ten thousand is still at or above the five thousand minimum. It is, so the withdrawal succeeds.

Step 3: Rajesh tries to withdraw another eight thousand. The policy computes the resulting balance of two thousand, which is below the minimum, so `allowsWithdrawal` returns false and the withdrawal is blocked. The rule was applied from the single policy, not a local hard-coded number.

Step 4: The maintenance service applies the monthly fee to Priya. It asks the policy `belowMinimumFee`, which sees four thousand is below five thousand and returns two percent of four thousand, eighty rupees. Priya is charged, driven by the same policy.

Step 5: The regulator raises the minimum to ten thousand. We create a new policy with that one value and the maintenance service immediately uses the new rule. In a real single-instance system this is one constant change in one place, and every flow picks it up — the essence of DRY.

```
2026-10-26 10:05:00 [INFO] === DRY: one rule, consulted by many flows ===
2026-10-26 10:05:00 [INFO] Withdrew Rs.990000 from SAV2001 -> balance Rs.10000
2026-10-26 10:05:00 [WARNING] Withdrawal Rs.8000 blocked for SAV2001 — would breach min balance Rs.5000
2026-10-26 10:05:00 [WARNING] CUR3001 below min balance -> fee Rs.80.00, balance Rs.3920.00
2026-10-26 10:05:00 [INFO] === Regulator raises minimum balance to Rs.10000 (single edit) ===
2026-10-26 10:05:00 [INFO] SAV2001 above min balance -> no fee
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
DRY stands for Don't Repeat Yourself, and it states that every piece of knowledge or business rule in a system should have a single, authoritative representation. The point is that when a rule changes, you change it in exactly one place rather than hunting through many copies and inevitably missing one. It is important to stress that DRY is about duplication of knowledge, not duplication of characters that merely look similar.

In my banking project the minimum-balance rule and the overdraft-fee calculation had been copy-pasted into the withdrawal flow, the monthly-maintenance flow, and the statement generator. When the regulator changed the minimum balance, a developer updated two of the three and missed the third, which produced wrong fees for customers. I fixed it by creating a single AccountPolicy class that owned those rules, and every flow consulted that policy instead of hard-coding numbers. After that, changing the minimum balance was a single safe edit that every flow picked up automatically.

The nuance I always raise is that you must distinguish true duplication from coincidental duplication. Two blocks that look identical today but represent different business rules are not real duplication, and merging them creates a false abstraction that becomes painful when the rules diverge and you start adding flags to the shared code. That is why experienced engineers say duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction, and you wait until the same knowledge genuinely repeats and changes together before unifying it.

In microservices, DRY has to be applied carefully because aggressively removing duplication can destroy the independence that microservices exist to give you. If every service imports one shared library for business logic, then changing that library forces every service to upgrade and redeploy together, and you have rebuilt a distributed monolith. So I apply DRY fully within a single service, but across service boundaries I deliberately tolerate some duplication to keep services autonomous. I only share stable, non-domain things like logging and security helpers, and even then as versioned libraries so each service upgrades on its own schedule. Where a rule truly must be consistent across services, I prefer the owning service to expose it through an API rather than everyone importing a shared implementation.
---

keyPoints: DRY: Do not Repeat Yourself — extract common logic
KISS: Keep It Simple — simplest solution that works
YAGNI: You Aren't Gonna Need It — do not build for imagined futures
Balance: DRY vs readability, YAGNI vs preparedness
